extracted.intended_audience: researchers and policy‑makers studying gender inequality in academia and research-funding agencies
extracted.subtask_short: analyzing gender bias in grant peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Critical synthesis and methodological guidance for studying whether and how applicant gender affects grant peer review and funding decisions, including identification of individual/systemic/social causes and recommendations for future research and policy. Targets analyses of peer review processes, outcome data, and grant scheme design across disciplines and countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant gender as a risk factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether applicants’ gender reliably predicts reviewer evaluations and funding outcomes (e.g. reviewer competence scores, funding rates, amounts awarded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical studies report mixed findings: some show women receive lower evaluations and less funding even when controlling for productivity, discipline, and seniority (e.g. Wennerås & Wold, 1997; Tamblyn et al., 2018); others using large-scale data or experiments show negligible or no gender effects (e.g. Marsh et al., 2009; Forscher et al., 2019). Analysts should examine both raw outcome differences and effects after controlling for covariates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual reviewer bias (conscious and unconscious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers’ stereotypical beliefs about competence and traits lead to differential evaluations of female and male applicants during peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes prescriptive/descriptive stereotype mechanisms (social role theory) and tendency to attribute agentic, standout wording (e.g. 'challenging', 'amazing') more to male applicants. Such bias can affect scores even when applicant productivity/track records are equivalent. Not strongly moderated by reviewer gender in existing studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic bias embedded in grant scheme design
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant program structures and evaluation criteria that advantage attributes more commonly held by men (e.g. bibliometric thresholds, emphasis on productivity, prestige indicators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systemic disadvantages for women (less citation, fewer first/last authorships, heavier teaching/admin loads, less institutional support) accumulate into weaker profiles under schemes that prioritise those metrics. Analysts should assess how scheme rules and criteria map onto gendered resource distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non‑blind review and applicant-identifying information
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of applicant identity (name, institution) in review materials allows reviewer biases (gender, race, institutional prestige) to influence evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many grant reviews are not blind, reviewers can be influenced by applicant gender, institutional size/prominence, and other identity cues. Studies using name manipulations (e.g. Forscher et al., 2019) provide experimental tests of this factor; double-blind review is a potential mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment dimensions used in peer review (e.g. 'quality of researcher' vs 'quality of proposal')
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific review criteria (such as quality of researcher, quality of proposal, knowledge utilisation) and how they are operationalised can show differential gender effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence (van der Lee & Ellemers, 2015; Witteman et al., 2019) shows gender disparities may appear on person-focused criteria (quality of researcher) but not on proposal-focused criteria. Evaluations should distinguish applicant-based from proposal-based criteria and analyse them separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalisation of productivity and bibliometric measures
rubrics_metrics.description: How researchers define and measure applicant productivity (publication counts, impact factors, h-index, composite indices) when controlling for merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variation in operationalisation (single measures vs composite indices that include past funding, h-index, sum of impact factors) leads to different results. Use comprehensive, appropriate indices and justify choices; be aware that incomplete measures may bias gender comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for contextual confounders (discipline, academic rank, application rates, subfield acceptance rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounting for third variables that co-vary with gender and funding success to avoid spurious associations (Simpson’s paradox).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stratify or control for applicant academic rank, discipline/subfield, application rates, and field-specific acceptance rates. Examples: differences vanish when controlling for subfield competitiveness or academic rank in some datasets (Albers, 2015; Waisbren et al., 2008).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish process-focused vs outcome-focused analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a study examines the peer review process (reviewer scores, language in critiques) or only final outcomes (funding awarded, amounts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focusing on only outcomes may obscure sources of bias; examining intermediate review steps clarifies whether bias arises in evaluations versus later decision stages. Combine both approaches where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological standardisation and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Need for standardised criteria and consistent operational definitions across studies to improve comparability and generalisability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant reviews lack standardised merit benchmarks; studies differ in inclusion criteria and variable definitions. Researchers should document operationalisations, justify variable choices, and where possible use multilevel/multivariate models to reflect real-world covariation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample size and generalisability
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of sufficient sample sizes and representative datasets to detect and generalise gender effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale, cross-disciplinary datasets afford more reliable effect estimates; some null findings arise from well-powered, generalisable studies. Small, case-specific studies may capture local effects but limit generalisability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability and reviewer training
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review reliability (agreement among reviewers) and the potential to improve it via training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review criticized for low reliability and reviewer agreement; training has been shown to improve inter-rater reliability (Sattler et al., 2015). Assess and report inter-rater metrics when analysing reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic/content analysis of reviewer critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing the language reviewers use (agentic vs communal traits, standout adjectives) to detect evaluative differences linked to applicant gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative linguistic methods and text mining can identify systematic differences in wording that reflect bias (Kaatz et al., 2015; Magua et al., 2017). Include qualitative analysis where informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of experimental / natural experiment designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Employing manipulations (e.g. name gender flips) or exploiting natural experiments to causally test gender effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controlled experiments (Forscher et al., 2019) and natural experiments at funding agencies (Witteman et al., 2019) provide stronger causal inference compared to observational comparisons; include such designs when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of social barriers and career-stage pipeline effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounting for family obligations, caregiving, teaching/admin loads, resource differentials, and lower application propensity among women that affect productivity and eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These social/contextual barriers reduce women’s submission and success rates; analyses should incorporate measures of application propensity, institutional support, and career-stage differences since when women reach senior rank their success may equal men’s (Holliday et al., 2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline- and field-specific analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognising that gender effects vary by discipline (e.g. STEM vs social sciences) and by field-level gender composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some fields show equity (social sciences) while male-dominated fields show larger gaps. Analysts should disaggregate by discipline/sub-discipline and interpret results in field-specific cultural contexts (e.g. role-model/network availability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing institutional and prestige effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluating the influence of applicants’ institutional size and prominence on review outcomes and how these interact with gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional affiliation can bias reviewers toward applicants from prominent institutions; because institutional resources are gender-unequal, this can produce indirect gender effects. Include institutional controls where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite, multilevel analytic approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of multilevel and multivariate statistical models that jointly account for applicant, reviewer, panel, scheme, and field-level variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-variable regressions can misrepresent complex relationships; multilevel models better capture nested data (applicants within panels within schemes) and have been recommended to resolve contradictory findings (Marsh et al., 2009).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy and practice recommendation: broader holistic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a comprehensive approach that examines individual biases, systemic grant-design factors, and social barriers to better understand and address gender inequities in funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations include stratifying datasets (by rank, field, application rate), standardising operationalisation, combining process and outcome analyses, using experimental designs when possible, and considering interventions (e.g. blinding, reviewer training, scheme redesign) to reduce bias.
